question: After the readiness RFC is accepted, should OpenClaw own the proposed four-profile v1 catalog with activation identity and release-tested conformance, including the reverse-proxy trust posture?
rationale: Choosing permanent support postures, authentication assurances, runtime identity semantics, and a release gate commits maintainers to product, security, and operational policy that cannot be inferred from implementation quality.

options.title: Accept the staged v1 contract
options.body: Approve the four opt-in profiles after the readiness dependency, retain activation identity, require security sign-off for reverse-proxy predicates, and phase in release-blocking conformance after an advisory period.

options.title: Narrow the first version
options.body: Accept profile selection and the initial catalog but defer activation identity and mandatory release gating to follow-up RFCs with separate owners.

options.title: Keep readiness unprofiled
options.body: Decline a core-owned named catalog and let operators compose explicit readiness criteria without an OpenClaw support-profile promise.

recommendation.title: Accept the staged v1 contract
recommendation.body: Approve the four opt-in profiles after the readiness dependency, retain activation identity, require security sign-off for reverse-proxy predicates, and phase in release-blocking conformance after an advisory period.

likelyOwner.reason: The merged stable-release-policy RFC provides the strongest available current-main ownership signal for the release-conformance commitment, though security and Gateway owners should also participate.
